content.text: Despite its dangers, radioactivity has many beneficial applications. From diagnosing diseases to treating cancer, from sterilising medical equipment to generating electricity, radioactive materials are essential tools in medicine, industry, and research. Understanding how and why specific isotopes are chosen for each application is important.

The choice of radioactive isotope for any application depends on three key factors: the type of radiation emitted (alpha, beta, or gamma), the half-life, and whether the source needs to be inside or outside the body or material being tested.
When selecting a radioactive isotope for a particular use, we consider:
(can it be incorporated into the body?)

Used for: bone scans, heart imaging, kidney function
Gamma rays penetrate the body and can be detected externally
Alpha/beta would be absorbed before reaching detectors
Positron meets electron, produces gamma rays
Used for cancer detection, brain studies
High-energy gamma rays directed at tumour
Multiple beams focus on tumour, sparing surrounding tissue
High dose to tumour, low dose to surroundings
Gamma rays kill bacteria and viruses
Equipment stays sterile until packaging opened
Radioactive source on one side, detector on other
Changes in thickness change count rate
Source on one side, detector on other

Used for checking fill levels remotely

Explain why technetium-99m is suitable for medical imaging.
It emits gamma radiation, which can penetrate the body and be detected from outside
Its half-life of 6 hours is long enough for the procedure but short enough to minimise radiation dose
It doesn't emit alpha or beta, which would increase patient dose without aiding detection
It can be attached to different molecules to target specific organs
A smoke detector uses americium-241. Explain why an alpha source is used rather than gamma.
Alpha particles are easily stopped by smoke particles, reducing the ionisation current and triggering the alarm
Alpha radiation cannot penetrate the plastic casing, making the detector safe
Gamma would pass through smoke without significant absorption, making detection less sensitive
Alpha's strong ionising ability creates the necessary current in normal conditions
Explain how radioactive tracers are used to detect a leak in an underground pipe.
A gamma-emitting radioactive tracer is added to the fluid in the pipe
A detector is moved along the ground above the pipe
Higher than normal readings indicate where the tracer has leaked out
A short half-life tracer is used so it decays quickly and doesn't contaminate the area
Gamma is used because it can penetrate the ground to reach the detector

When explaining why a particular isotope is chosen for an application, always state: (1) the type of radiation it emits and why that type is suitable, and (2) whether its half-life is appropriate for the task. For example, a medical tracer needs gamma radiation (penetrates the body) and a short half-life (reduces patient dose).
— Food exposed to radiation doesn't become radioactive. The radiation kills bacteria but doesn't remain.
"Any radioactive isotope can be used for any purpose"
— The type of radiation, half-life, and chemical properties must match the application.
— It carries risks, but these are carefully balanced against benefits. Doses are kept as low as reasonably achievable.
— The alpha source is safely contained and cannot harm you unless the detector is broken open and the source ingested.
"Radioactive tracers stay in the body forever"
— Short half-life tracers decay quickly, and the body also eliminates them naturally.
Short half-life: medical tracers, leak detection (limits exposure)
Long half-life: smoke detectors, thickness gauges (no frequent replacement)
Choice depends on: penetration needed, detection method, safety considerations
